land.text: the Hindush infobox gives 'Preceded by: Sindhu-Sauvira'; the Sindhu-Sauvira page: its territory was 'organised into the satrapy (province) of Hindush', 'southern border being the Indian Ocean and its northern border being the Punjab around Multan'

predecessors.note: Sindhu-Sauvira has a dossier in this batch (-1000..-518); its extent is the Sindhu-Sauvira page's, which matches the Hindush page's 'lower and central Indus basin'.

land.text: the Taksasila country east of the Indus that the Gandhara dossier (sa-01-a) gives to the Achaemenids in -518

predecessors.note: Pages disagree on whether Taxila was Hindush or Gandara (see notes); the Gandara page says 'Taxila in the former Hindush satrapy'.

land.text: 'Macedonian Empire annexes northwestern India' (infobox of the Indian campaign page); Alexander made Peithon viceroy of 'the land extending from the confluence of the Indus and Acesines as far as the sea'

successors.note: Taxila passed to Alexander's ally Ambhi (Taxiles) in -326, the Sindh and Multan country in -325.

capitals.name: Bhir Mound, Taxila (Takshashila)
capitals.note: The conquest page names 'Bhir Mound in Takshashila (Taxila)' as Hindush's capital; the Hindush page says only that the province 'ruled from Sindimana which was probably the capital'. Coordinates are the site's location (the pages give none).

capitals.name: Sindimana (Sindomana, Sehwan)
capitals.note: Probable capital on the Hindush page; the Sehwan page identifies Sindomana with Sehwan on the west bank of the Indus and says it was the capital of King Sambos, defeated by Alexander in 326 BC. Listed once for the last year, when the Taxila seat is gone; the Hindush page does not date its use.

correction.text: 'the lower and central Indus basin' / 'present-day Sindh and the southern Punjab in Pakistan' (Hindush page): Sindh and the Multan country together with Taxila and the land between the Indus and the Jhelum, which the conquest page makes Hindush's capital district ('Bhir Mound in Takshashila') with 'the Indus River to the west, and the Jhelum River in the south and east'; the Gandara page has 'Ambhi, ruler of Taxila in the former Hindush satrapy'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria has no Hindush row; the Achaemenid Empire row of the Iran group draws only western Sindh in -500..-405, 254 of Sindh's 562 cells, and nothing south of 29.5N from -404 to -327, though this page says the province 'existed as a province for approximately two centuries'). The infobox gives no area; the shape resolves to about 235,000 km2. The page gives two views of the extent (Sindh and southern Punjab; or Punjab, 'the region of Taxila and Western Punjab' on the conquest page); the shape takes both.

correction.text: 'the lower and central Indus basin' / 'present-day Sindh and the southern Punjab in Pakistan' (Hindush page): Sindh and the Multan country

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. Taxila ('Omphis (Ambhi), ruler of Taxila, whose kingdom extended from the Indus to the Jhelum, complied') leaves in the spring of 326, leaving Sindh and the Multan country until Alexander's conquest of the lower Indus (the Sehwan page: Sambos 'defeated by Alexander ... in 326 BC'; the Peithon page: viceroy 'around 325 BC'). About 208,000 km2.

region.text: 'the lower and central Indus basin' / 'present-day Sindh and the southern Punjab in Pakistan' (Hindush page): Sindh and the Multan country

ledger.note: 518 BCE: Darius conquers Sindhu-Sauvira and organises it as the satrapy of Hindush. 'In 518 BCE, Sindhu-Sauvira was conquered by the Persian Achaemenid Empire under Darius I' and 'organised into the satrapy (province) of Hindush', its extent 'the Indian Ocean' in the south to 'the Punjab around Multan' in the north. The Hindush infobox has 'Persian conquest of the Indus Valley: c. 513 BCE' and the Indian-campaign page 'c. 515 BC'; Darius's push to the Jhelum is 'around 518 BCE' on the conquest page.

region.text: Taxila and the land between the Indus and the Jhelum, which the conquest page makes Hindush's capital district ('Bhir Mound in Takshashila') with 'the Indus River to the west, and the Jhelum River in the south and east'; the Gandara page has 'Ambhi, ruler of Taxila in the former Hindush satrapy'

ledger.note: 518 BCE: Taxila and the Indus-Jhelum country join Hindush (the Hindush page has c. 513 BCE for the conquest). The conquest page names 'Bhir Mound in Takshashila (Taxila)' as the capital of Hindush, bounded by 'the Indus River to the west, and the Jhelum River in the south and east'; the Gandhara dossier (sa-01-a) loses the Taksasila country in -518 and names the Achaemenid Empire as heir; this event is the part of it that belongs to the satrapy.

region.text: Taxila and the land between the Indus and the Jhelum, which the conquest page makes Hindush's capital district ('Bhir Mound in Takshashila') with 'the Indus River to the west, and the Jhelum River in the south and east'; the Gandara page has 'Ambhi, ruler of Taxila in the former Hindush satrapy'

ledger.note: 326 BCE: Taxila submits to Alexander. 'Omphis (Indic: Ambhi), ruler of Taxila, whose kingdom extended from the Indus to the Jhelum (Greek: Hydaspes), complied'; 'In early spring of the next year [326], he combined his forces and allied with Taxiles'. The page gives no year for the submission itself; the Hydaspes battle is 'July 326 BC'. The Gandara page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandara_(Achaemenid_province)) has 'Ambhi, ruler of Taxila in the former Hindush satrapy'. Taxila stays under its own king as Alexander's ally.

region.text: the Sindh and Multan country of Hindush, which Alexander's campaign of 327-325 BC annexed: 'Macedonian Empire annexes northwestern India'

ledger.note: 325 BCE: Alexander makes Peithon viceroy of the Indus. 'Alexander named him viceroy of the Indus area, around 325 BC', 'the land extending from the confluence of the Indus and Acesines as far as the sea'. The Indian-campaign page: 'began in 327 BC and lasted until 325 BC', Peithon satrap 'until 316 BC', the Malli 'in modern-day Multan' conquered; the Sehwan page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sehwan_Sharif) dates the defeat of Sambos at Sindomana to 326 BC.

wars.name: Achaemenid conquest of the Indus Valley

zones.text: the Indus valley from Taxila to the sea

wars.outcome: Persian victory: Gandara under Cyrus (c. 535 BCE), then Darius's push 'up to the Jhelum River' (c. 518 BCE) and the Indus satrapy Hindush (518 on the Sindhu-Sauvira page, 'c. 513 BCE' on the Hindush page).
wars.note: Infobox date 'c. 535/518 BCE - 323 BCE'. The page does not date the creation of either satrapy; Hindush is listed among Darius's provinces by the end of his reign (486 BCE). Trimmed by the reviewer (2026-10-18) to -518, the year of Darius's push 'up to the Jhelum River' on the conquest page, so that the war lies inside this dossier's life (-518..-325); the c. 535 phase under Cyrus is in gandara's wars.

wars.name: Indian campaign of Alexander the Great

zones.text: Taxila, the Multan country of the Malli and the lower Indus down to Patala

wars.outcome: Macedonian victory: 'Macedonian Empire annexes northwestern India'; Peithon governs the Indus to 316 BC.
wars.note: Hindush is listed as the land fought over; by 326 the Persian administration had gone and the opponents were local rulers (Sambos, the Malli, Musicanus c. 323 BC). The page gives no year for Taxila's submission, the Malli or Patala.

certainty.note: The pages disagree on the satrapy's extent (Sindh and southern Punjab, or the Taxila-Jhelum country) and on its capital (Sindimana, Bhir Mound); every edge is approximate.

notes: Type colony: a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire (family persia), to be drawn as the empire's vassal tint; the Achaemenid dossier of the Iran group should carry the matching relation. Cliopatria has no row: the Achaemenid Empire row draws part of Sindh in -500..-405 and not from -404 to -327, which the Hindush page contradicts. Disagreement between pages: the Hindush page puts the province in 'present-day Sindh and the southern Punjab' with Sindimana (Sehwan) as probable capital (the Sindhu-Sauvira page agrees on the extent, from the sea to the Punjab around Multan) and says 'some authors consider that Hindush may have been located in the Punjab region'; the conquest page makes Taxila the capital with the Indus and Jhelum as bounds; the Gandara page calls Taxila 'the former Hindush satrapy'. The shape unites both readings; a gap-filler should open a specialist source. Dates: the start is 518, the year of the Sindhu-Sauvira page's conquest and of the conquest page's push to the Jhelum; the Hindush infobox has c. 513 and the Indian-campaign page c. 515 (both within five years); the end is the Peithon page's c. 325 (the Sehwan page has Alexander at Sindomana in 326). The Persian rulers are not a ruler strip: the Hindush infobox lists Darius I (513-499) and Darius III (336-330) only as kings of the empire. After the Persian collapse (Gaugamela 331; the Hindush page says only that the province remained until Alexander) the Indus lands were held by local kings (Ambhi, Sambos, Musicanus); no page dates the end of Persian control there, so the keyframe runs to -327. Sindhu-Sauvira (the infobox predecessor) has its own dossier in this batch. Gazetteer: Sehwan (26.43N 67.86E) is not a place; the capitals use its coordinates.
